lead.headline: Four Countries Team Up to Keep Supplies Flowing
lead.deck: The Quad met in Manila and made deals on the materials inside batteries.
body: Inside every phone battery are small amounts of materials such as lithium and cobalt. Electric cars need them too. These are called critical minerals: modern devices can’t do without them, but they can be hard to get.

That is why four leaders met in Manila, in the Philippines, on Tuesday: Donald Trump of the United States, Narendra Modi of India, Sanae Takaichi of Japan and Anthony Albanese of Australia. Their group is called the Quad.

Trump announced new deals on critical minerals. He said they would stop “coercion by any single foreign supplier.” Coercion means forcing someone to do something. He did not name the minerals, who signed, or China, which dominates the world’s supply of rare earths.
The leaders also agreed that their patrol planes will fly together over the sea in 2027, and they will spend more than $85 million to help the region use trusted AI.

world.headline: A Message to Voyager 1 Now Takes a Whole Day
world.deck: The spacecraft launched in 1977 reaches one light-day from Earth today.
body: In one day, light travels about 25.89 billion kilometres, a distance called a light-day. Today, NASA’s Voyager 1 becomes the first spacecraft to get that far from Earth.

That means a radio message sent from Earth needs a full 24 hours to reach it, and its reply needs another 24 hours to come back. Voyager 1 was launched in 1977 to fly past Jupiter and Saturn, and it is still sending data from beyond the planets. It speeds along at about 17 kilometres every second.

Its power is slowly fading, so engineers have switched off parts to save energy. Of the 10 science instruments it launched with, only 2 still work, and the team thinks it has enough power to keep going until about the early 2030s. NASA’s telescopes in Canberra, California and Madrid keep track of it. On Tuesday evening, NASA invited people to flash lights in Morse code after sunset to celebrate.

us.headline: After Planes Stopped, America Pauses a Computer Upgrade
us.deck: Air traffic control is changing how it fixes its equipment.
body: Last Friday, flights across America were stopped for nearly five hours. The trouble began when a new router, a box that links computers together, was installed at a site in El Dorado, Arkansas.

After that router went in, the system was flooded with about 1,000 attempts to connect every four to five seconds. That knocked out radio and radar in 17 of the country’s 22 regional air traffic control centres. The full cause is still being studied.

On Tuesday, the Federal Aviation Administration said it is pausing new router installs. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the agency may need to rethink when it does upgrades, because this work was done in the daytime.
us.why: When one box can stop flights everywhere, it shows why careful testing matters before families pack for a trip.
also: Duffy has asked Congress for $50 billion to upgrade the ageing air traffic system.

india.headline: Families on India’s East Coast Get Ready for Cyclone Akvan
india.deck: A strong storm should reach Andhra Pradesh around noon on Friday.
body: A cyclone is a giant spinning storm that grows over warm sea. Cyclone Akvan is over the Bay of Bengal, and India’s weather office, the IMD, expects it to keep growing stronger before it reaches land. Late on Monday, it was about 670 km from the port city of Visakhapatnam.

The IMD says it should cross the coast of Andhra Pradesh, between Nellore and Tuni, around noon on Friday. Winds could blow at 120 to 130 km an hour, with gusts up to 145, and heavy rain is expected in parts of Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and Tamil Nadu.

Families are already acting on the warnings. Odisha has started moving people out of risky areas, and fishermen have been told to stay off the sea until Friday. The IMD has warned of extensive damage in coastal parts of Andhra Pradesh. The storm’s name, Akvan, was suggested by Iran, one of 13 countries that share a list of storm names.
india.why: Warnings days ahead give families time to pack, move and stay safe, which is how storms do less harm.

lines.text: Good morning, and welcome to The Breakfast Table for Wednesday, November 18. Today: what’s inside your batteries, a spacecraft a whole day away, and a storm families are getting ready for.
Let’s start with batteries. Why were world leaders talking about them?

Phone batteries hold small amounts of materials such as lithium and cobalt, and electric cars need them too. They’re called critical minerals, because modern devices can’t do without them, but they can be hard to get.
And who met to talk about them?

Four leaders, from the United States, India, Japan and Australia, met in Manila on Tuesday. Together they’re called the Quad. President Trump announced new deals on critical minerals. He said they would stop coercion by any single foreign supplier. Coercion means forcing someone to do something.
Did they agree on anything else?
Yes. Their patrol planes will fly together over the sea in 2027. And they will spend more than 85 million dollars to help the region use trusted AI.
Now, a spacecraft that’s a whole day away. What does that mean?
In one day, light travels about 25.89 billion kilometres. That distance is called a light-day. Today, NASA’s Voyager 1 becomes the first spacecraft to get that far from Earth.
So if I sent it a message?

Your radio message would need a full 24 hours to reach it, and the reply would need another 24 hours to come back. Voyager 1 was launched in 1977 to fly past Jupiter and Saturn, and it’s still sending data from beyond the planets.
Is it still working well after all that time?
Its power is slowly fading, so engineers have switched off parts to save energy. Of the 10 science instruments it launched with, 2 still work.
Finally, a storm in India. What’s happening?

A cyclone is a giant spinning storm that grows over warm sea. Cyclone Akvan is over the Bay of Bengal, and India’s weather office expects it to cross the coast of Andhra Pradesh around noon on Friday.
How strong could it be?

Winds could blow at 120 to 130 kilometres an hour, with gusts up to 145. The good news is that warnings came days ahead. Odisha has started moving people out of risky areas, and fishermen have been told to stay off the sea until Friday.
